svg.text: KYC / eKYC — DigiLocker (Surepass) & AEPS eKYC
InstantMudra Enterprises Admin Portal
DigiLocker = Surepass — one integration, two names in the top-level docs
DigilockerController (/api/digilocker) → DigilockerServiceImpl → https://kyc-api.surepass.app/api/v1/digilocker/*
Both call sites use one static bearer token (@Value("${surepass.digilocker.token}")) — "DigiLocker" and "Surepass" in the top-level review are the same vendor, not two.
⚠ DigilockerServiceImpl — static token, zero response handling
Static, non-refreshing bearer token
digilockerToken injected once from application.properties
(a long-lived Surepass JWT — documented, masked, in Module 1).
No refresh/regeneration logic anywhere in this class — when
the token expires, every DigiLocker call fails until someone
manually rotates the config value.
No response/error handling
return response.getBody();
— both initializeDigilocker() and downloadAadhaar()
return the raw body directly: no HTTP status check, no
null check, no try/catch. A vendor error surfaces as an
unhandled exception or a silent null downstream.
⚠ CRITICAL — authenticated IDOR exposing Aadhaar data
GET /api/digilocker/download-aadhaar/{clientId}
Requires a valid AESFilter-passed token — this path is absent from both whitelists (Module 4), so it's not anonymously public.
But nothing in DigilockerController or DigilockerServiceImpl checks that the requested clientId belongs to the caller's own
KYC session or hierarchy — clientId is taken as a raw path variable and forwarded straight to Surepass.
Any authenticated user — any hierarchy level — can retrieve any OTHER person's Aadhaar data (name, photo, DOB, address)
by supplying a different clientId. This is more consequential than a wallet-balance IDOR: Aadhaar is government-ID PII.
AepsEkycOrchestrator — correctly wired, injected, and never called
AepsEkycController autowires both aepsEkycOrchestrator and aepsEkycService — but all 5 endpoints
(send-otp, validate-otp, resend-otp, biometric, validate-otp-biometric) call only aepsEkycService.XXX(req).
Confirmed by search: "AepsEkycOrchestrator" appears in exactly 2 files — its own definition, and this unused @Autowired field.
AepsEkycOrchestrator itself is correctly built: resolves VendorRouting → VendorCredentials → AepsVendorFactory → calls the
resolved vendor. Unlike Module 5's AEPS-transaction bypass (a separate legacy class did the work), here the dead orchestrator
was wired into the dependency graph and simply never invoked — someone injected it and never wrote the call.
AepsEkycServiceImpl duplicates the orchestrator's vendor-routing logic independently
The class that's actually called resolves VendorRouting itself — vendorRoutingRepository.findBySubProductId(...) appears at
5 separate call sites within AepsEkycServiceImpl (624 lines), each duplicating what AepsEkycOrchestrator already does once.
Same "pattern exists, real traffic bypasses it" shape documented for AEPS transactions in Module 5 — now confirmed for eKYC too.
Standard / correctly wired
Flagged risk / dead code / duplication
Critical — confirmed PII-exposure gap
Generated from source review — InstantMudra Enterprises Admin Portal — module 10 of the architecture documentation set
